title: Chayei Sarah: the life of Sarah
hook: a portion called "the life of Sarah" begins with her death

segments.voice: Yesterday, hineni: Abraham answering here I am, to God, to his son, to the angel. Your line was here I am. Who did you show up for? Day one hundred eighty-one.

Think about the last funeral you went to. At some point, someone stood up and said: let's not talk about how she died. Let's talk about how she lived. The stories came out. The way she laughed. The thing she always cooked. This week's Torah portion does the same thing, in its name. It's called Chayei Sarah, the life of Sarah. And its very first lines tell us that Sarah has died. Every week, Jews read a portion named for her life that opens with her death. Today: why the name is life.
screen: `WHAT PEOPLE SAY AT A FUNERAL.` → `CHAYEI SARAH: THE LIFE OF SARAH.` → `IT OPENS WITH HER DEATH.`

segments.voice: Portions take their names from their first important words, and here the first words are these. In the Jewish Publication Society's old translation: "And the life of Sarah was a hundred and seven and twenty years; these were the years of the life of Sarah." Notice it doesn't say Sarah died at a hundred and twenty-seven. It says her life was that long, and then it says so again. The Hebrew counts it strangely, too: a hundred years, and twenty years, and seven years, each with its own word for years. Rashi, the great medieval teacher, read that slowly. He said each stage of her life is counted on its own because each was whole. At a hundred she was as free of wrongdoing as she had been at twenty, and at twenty as lovely as at seven. And then that closing phrase, these were the years of the life of Sarah: Rashi says all of them were equally good. Not only the famous ones. The waiting years, the laughing year, the old years. There's a harder side, too. The portion comes right after Abraham takes Isaac up the mountain, and an old midrash connects the two: Sarah died, it says, when she heard what had happened to her son. The text itself is silent about that. What the text does say is that Abraham came to mourn for Sarah, and to weep for her. So the portion holds both things. A real death, real grief, and a name that points past it. The rabbis loved that choice. When you remember someone, you get to choose which word goes on the door. The Torah chose life.
screen: `THE LIFE OF SARAH WAS…` · `A HUNDRED, TWENTY AND SEVEN YEARS.` · `ALL HER YEARS WERE GOOD.` · `ABRAHAM CAME TO MOURN AND WEEP.` · then, large: `THE PORTION IS CALLED LIFE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember a life, not just a death. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone you've lost, a grandparent, a friend, a teacher, even a pet. Let yourself skip past the ending for a moment. Find one ordinary scene from their life. A kitchen. A car ride. Something they always said. Stay in that scene. Let them be alive in it for these two minutes. The bell holds the time.
Chayei Sarah. The life of Sarah: a Torah portion that opens with her death, and is named for her life. Chayim, life, is the same word in the toast l'chaim.
Your line: the portion is called life. Today, tell someone one story about a person you miss, a story from their living, not their dying. Day one hundred eighty-one.

howItsDone: Chayei Sarah is read in synagogues each autumn, and many Jews remember loved ones by telling stories of their lives at shivah, the week of mourning, and on each yahrzeit, the anniversary of a death.

fork.setup: you're naming a Torah portion. its first story is Sarah's death and burial. what do you call it?
fork.reveal: it's Chayei Sarah, the life of Sarah, from its first words. the name points past the death to the life.

original.note: Hebrew: the life of Sarah. chayei comes from chayim, life, as in l'chaim.

trapdoor: what you thought: a portion about Sarah's funeral.
what it means: a portion named for her life, remembering every stage of it as whole.
what a scholar hears: Genesis 23:1 repeats the word for years for each part of her age; Rashi reads it as each stage of her life being good.

notes: Confirm the JPS 1917 wording of Genesis 23:1.
Rashi on 23:1 (each stage counted separately; at 100 like 20 in sin, at 20 like 7 in beauty; 'all equally good') paraphrased from memory; confirm.
The midrash linking Sarah's death to the binding of Isaac is cited to Genesis Rabbah 58:5 and appears in Rashi on 23:2; confirm the citation.
'Portions take their names from their first important words' is a simplification; confirm framing.
